Its stored run used the deterministic keyword baseline on 3,610 US G60 feedback records, producing 2,518 signals and seven requirement candidates. All 21 pairwise score comparisons remain unresolved because the score ranges overlap. Customer impact, business criteria, engineering feasibility, and cost still lack reviewed inputs; no PM decisions are recorded.

The current database passed reconciliation of 10,128 feedback IDs and 13,771 annotation rows, validation of all 2,518 exact citation spans, unique-ID recurrence checks, and audit-chain validation. All 12 software tests passed. A smoke check processed 200 F70 and 200 G70 records, but extraction accuracy, citation entailment, and ranking quality have **not** been measured against adjudicated examples. See [TASKS.md](</D:/ChatGPT/bmw challenge/TASKS.md>) and [DECISION_ENGINE.md](</D:/ChatGPT/bmw challenge/docs/DECISION_ENGINE.md>).

Two operational gaps surfaced: CLI replay fails under the Windows default text encoding, although it succeeds with UTF-8 output; and the [UI](</D:/ChatGPT/bmw challenge/ui/app.py>) defaults to a different database path from the populated `decision_engine_v2.db`. The next decision-quality step is to freeze and adjudicate the evaluation set, then test grounding and ranking sensitivity.
explain how the decision engine works

The engine turns feedback into **reviewable requirement candidates**, then calculates a policy-dependent value range for each one.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Supplied feedback] --> B[Group rows by feedback ID]
  B --> C[Extract signals with exact text spans]
  C --> D[Group signals by customer outcome]
  D --> E[Count unique supporting records]
  E --> F[Calculate score ranges]
  F --> G[PM review and audit history]
```

The first safeguard is the evidence unit. One feedback ID can have several annotation rows, but it counts only once toward a given requirement’s reach. The engine retains the original row locations and separates complaints and aspirations from praise and descriptive context. It checks that cited text spans exist in the stored record. **Whether a span actually supports the drafted claim still needs human review.**

Scoring currently uses an unapproved, equal-weight policy with four criteria: customer impact, evidence-backed reach, strategic contribution, and competitive or future need. Reach is calculated from supporting IDs divided by eligible IDs in the requirement’s scope, using a declared 5% saturation point. Unknown criteria keep their weight and contribute a possible range instead of being guessed or dropped. Feasibility and cost stay separate from the value score.

For example, the stored “Software Reliability” candidate has 277 supporting IDs among 3,610 eligible US G60 IDs. That exceeds the seed policy’s 5% reach threshold, so reach contributes 25 points. The other three criteria are unknown, yielding a **25–100 scenario range**. Every current candidate’s range overlaps every other candidate’s, so the displayed lower-bound order is a triage view, not a defensible winner.

A PM can approve, reject, defer, challenge, or edit a candidate with a rationale. An edit creates a new revision; the database records decisions and an audit chain so earlier states can be replayed. A challenge does not yet automatically gather new evidence or recompute an argument. The stored run used a keyword baseline, and no human-rated extraction or ranking accuracy has been measured.

A local decision-support prototype for turning customer evidence into reviewable requirements for future BMW vehicles. The first working scope is 5 Series G60 feedback from the US; F70 and G70 are used to check whether the method transfers to other vehicles.

1. **Preserve and reconcile evidence.** Keep the supplied files unchanged and record source hashes, spreadsheet rows, cells, pages, and any cleaning transformations. Multiple annotation rows for one feedback ID remain one feedback record for recurrence counts.
